passages.title: Glorify the Most High who creates and ordains
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open Sūrat al-Aʿlā with a single command — glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High — and then give the reasons why He alone deserves that glorification: He creates and perfects, He measures and guides, He brings forth life, and He brings that life to its appointed end. What binds the passage together is the movement from the command in ayah 1 to the portrait of the Lord in ayat 2–5: each clause is another facet of *al-Aʿlā*, "the Most High", so that by ayah 5 the believer knows exactly Who it is he has been told to glorify.

## A sūrah the Prophet ﷺ loved

Ibn Kathir establishes that this sūrah was revealed in Makkah before the migration. His proof is a narration recorded by al-Bukhari from al-Barāʾ bin ʿĀzib, who describes the Companions arriving in Madinah in waves — Musʿab bin ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktūm first, teaching people the Qurʼān, then ʿAmmār, Bilāl and Saʿd, then ʿUmar with twenty men, and finally the Prophet ﷺ himself, whose arrival made the people of Madinah happier than anything al-Barāʾ had ever seen, with even the children crying out, "This is the Messenger of Allah who has come." Al-Barāʾ notes that before the Prophet ﷺ ever arrived, he had already learned to recite *Sabbiḥisma Rabbika l-Aʿlā* — the sūrah had reached Madinah ahead of its Prophet ﷺ.

The Prophet's ﷺ own attachment to this sūrah runs through his prayer life, and Ibn Kathir gathers the evidence under the sūrah's virtues. It is confirmed in the Two Sahihs that he said to Muʿādh, "Why didn't you recite 'Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High', 'By the sun and its brightness', and 'By the night when it envelopes.'" Imam Ahmad recorded from al-Nuʿmān bin Bashīr — with Muslim also recording it in his Sahih, as well as Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasaʼi and Ibn Majah — that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite Sūrat al-Aʿlā and Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah in the two ʿĪd prayers and in Jumuʿah, and if ʿĪd fell on a Friday he would recite them in both prayers of that day. Imam Ahmad also recorded in his Musnad, on the authority of Ubayy bin Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Abzā and ʿĀʼishah, that he used to recite this sūrah together with *Qul yā ayyuhal-kāfirūn* and *Qul huwallāhu aḥad*.

## Answering the command as you recite it

The first ayah is a command, and the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions treated it as one to be obeyed on the spot. Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited *Sabbiḥisma Rabbika l-Aʿlā*, he would respond: **Subḥāna Rabbiya l-Aʿlā** — "Glory to my Lord, the Most High." Qatādah relates the same practice from the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarīr recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās did likewise, just as he would answer the end of Sūrat al-Qiyāmah — "Is not He able to give life to the dead?" (75:40) — with "Glory to You, of course." The recitation was a conversation: Allah commands glorification, and the reciter glorifies then and there.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this was the practice of the noble Companions generally — ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn Zubayr, Abū Mūsā and ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd — citing al-Qurṭubī, and notes the scholars' ruling that saying it is commendable, outside of the formal prayer. It also relates from ʿUqbah Ibn ʿĀmir al-Juhanī that when this sūrah was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ instructed that this tasbīḥ be said in the prostrations.

## What "glorify the Name" asks of you

*Tasbīḥ* means to pronounce the purity of Allah — to declare Him free of every deficiency and everything unbecoming of His sublime status. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what it means that the *Name* is glorified: when the name of Allah is pronounced, it must be with utmost humility and respect, and Allah is to be called only by the names He Himself has stated or taught His Prophet ﷺ — it is not permitted to invent names for Him.

From this, Maʿārif (citing al-Qurṭubī) derives a practical ruling many people trip over without noticing: some names belong exclusively to Allah, and calling a human being by them contradicts declaring His purity. So when people shorten names like ʿAbdur-Raḥmān, ʿAbdur-Razzāq, ʿAbdul-Ghaffār or ʿAbdul-Quddūs to just "Raḥmān", "Razzāq", "Ghaffār" or "Quddūs" — dropping the "ʿAbd" ("slave of") — both speaker and listener fall into a sin committed casually, day and night, for no gain at all.

Maʿārif also records a second reading of *ism* here: some commentators, again cited via al-Qurṭubī, held that *ism* in this verse does not mean "name" but refers to the very Being (*Dhāt*) of Allah Himself — an interpretation Arabic usage allows. Their evidence is the tasbīḥ we are instructed to recite in prostration: "I pronounce the purity of my most exalted Lord," not "…of the name of my Lord." Both readings are transmitted; on either one, the command is to exalt Allah above all else.

## The portrait of the Most High: from creation to its appointed end

Having commanded glorification, the passage now shows Who is being glorified, in one continuous sweep — created, perfected, measured, guided, brought forth, brought to an end. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the verbs of ayat 2 and 3 as four attributes of the Most Exalted Lord, each deliberately chosen, and ayat 4 and 5 then display those same attributes at work in a single field of grass.

**Khalaqa — "Who created."** This is not mere making or manufacturing. Maʿārif insists on the word's deeper significance: to bring something out of pure non-existence into existence without any pre-existing matter. That is creation in its true sense, and it is within no one's power but Allah's.

**Fa-sawwā — "then perfected."** From *taswiyah*, "to make well, to make even." Ibn Kathir puts it simply: He fashioned every creation in the best of forms. Maʿārif dwells on the human body as the visible proof — the joints of fingers and toes with their springy connective tissues allowing bending and folding, the symmetry and balance of every limb and organ — enough, it says, to baffle the imagination and to convince anyone of the consummate wisdom and power of the Creator.

**Qaddara — "Who measured."** From *taqdīr*: to determine, measure, balance, decree. Nothing in the world was created without purpose; everything is endowed with capacities fitted exactly to its function — sky, stars, lightning, rain, humans, animals, vegetation, minerals. Ibn Kathir explains that He decreed a set measure and guided the creation to it, and connects this to the divine decree itself, citing what is confirmed in Sahih Muslim on the authority of ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, Allah ordained the measure of all creation fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was over the water."

**Fa-hadā — "then guided."** The Creator did not make things and abandon them to work out their functions alone. Mujāhid said: "He guided man to distress and happiness, and he guided the cattle to their pastures" — guidance covering both man's moral road and the animal's instinct. Ibn Kathir pairs this ayah with Mūsā's answer to Firʿawn: "Our Lord is He Who gave to each thing its form and nature, then guided it aright" (20:50). Maʿārif paints the picture at full width: since the inception of creation the skies, the earth, the stars and planets, mountains and oceans have performed their functions without failure or deviation; birds, beasts and insects find their food and their habitats with no teacher, no school — "their education and training comes directly from the Creator of the universe." Even human science, it adds, is part of this *hadā*: Allah equipped man with intelligence to mine mountains, dive into oceans, and combine wood, iron and copper into new things. Science creates nothing; it only discovers how to use what Allah created, and the very capacity for that discovery is His gift — a reality, Maʿārif laments, that scientists grow ever more blind to.

Then, without a pause, the passage narrows all of this to one vivid image. The Lord who measures and guides is the One who "brings forth the pasture" — Ibn Kathir: all types of vegetation and crops — "then makes it dark stubble." Ibn ʿAbbās explained the stubble as "dried up and altered," and Mujāhid, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd said the same.

Maʿārif opens up the rare words. *Marʿā* is pasturage — land where grass grows and animals graze. *Ghuthāʼ* refers to stubble, and to the scum borne upon the surface of a torrent. *Aḥwā* comes from a root denoting the kind of blackness that comes over dense vegetation. The verse, Maʿārif says, depicts the Divine power and wisdom at work in herbage and vegetation: He grows the green vegetation, then gradually turns it black, and it loses its freshness.

And here the passage turns its gaze on the reader. Maʿārif says this image "directs man's attention also to his end": the body radiating with health, beauty and alertness is a divine gift — but its tenure is limited, and eventually it will come to an end. The same Lord who raises the green pasture also appoints its withering; the same is true of you. The One who does all of this — who creates, perfects, measures, guides, brings forth and brings to an end — is *al-Aʿlā*, the Most High, and the fitting response is the one ayah 1 commanded and the Prophet ﷺ modeled: *Subḥāna Rabbiya l-Aʿlā*.

passages.title: Promises to the Prophet: recitation preserved, path eased
passages.tafsir:
## Promises before a commission

After opening with the command to glorify Allah and four ayat describing His creative power — He who created, proportioned, measured, guided, and brings forth pasture — the sūrah now turns directly to the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the sequence: in the preceding verses Allah depicted the manifestation of His Omnipotence and wisdom; then, before the guidelines concerning his prophetic obligation are put forth, the Prophet ﷺ is first given "the cheerful news of making his task easier." Only after this reassurance does the command come in ayah 9: "Therefore remind."

## "We will make you recite, so you will not forget" (ayah 6)

To feel the force of this promise, you need the scene behind it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls that when the Qurʼan was first being revealed, as Jibraʼil (peace be upon him) began to recite, the Prophet ﷺ would hurry to repeat the words after him, anxious that a word or sentence might slip away. He was told not to make haste — to wait until the angel had delivered the whole message and then repeat it, assured that its preservation was a Divine arrangement and nothing would be lost. Ayah 6 states that arrangement "still more plainly": *We* will make you recite, and *you will not forget*.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way: this is Allah informing and promising the Prophet ﷺ that He will teach him a recitation he will not forget.

## "Except what Allah wills" (ayah 7) — what does the exception mean?

The promise carries one exception, and the scholars explained it in two ways — both preserved in the sources.

**The abrogation reading.** Qatadah, as Ibn Kathir cites him, said simply: "The Prophet did not forget anything except what Allah willed." Ibn Kathir explains the sense: 'do not forget what We teach you to recite, except what Allah wills, which He removes — and there is no sin on your leaving it off.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops this: while Allah made the Prophet ﷺ remember all of the Qurʼan, certain verses were caused to be forgotten because they had been abrogated — done by Allah's command, and never without reason. This abrogation could happen in more than one way: sometimes a second clear injunction was revealed contrary to the first; at other times a verse was obliterated from the memory of the Prophet ﷺ and of all other Muslims together. The Qurʼan itself describes this: "Whenever We abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten" (2:106). So the exception does not weaken the promise — even the "forgetting" was a deliberate act of the same Lord who preserves the rest.

**The temporary-lapse reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that some scholars understood the exception differently: Allah may for some reason blot a verse temporarily from the Prophet's ﷺ memory, and he then remembers it again. In support, it relates (citing Qurtubi) that one day the Prophet ﷺ recited a sūrah but omitted one of its verses. Ubayy Ibn Kaʿb, one of his scribes, was present and thought the verse might have been abrogated; when he asked, the Prophet ﷺ told him it was not abrogated but had been omitted by mistake. On this reading, a momentary lapse followed by recall does not contradict the promise — it is precisely the exception the ayah allows for. Maʿārif ends the discussion with the words: "Allah knows best."

The ayah then seals the matter: **"Indeed He knows what is apparent and what is hidden."** Ibn Kathir explains: Allah knows what His creatures do openly and what they conceal, whether words or deeds — none of it is hidden from Him. The One who guarantees the Qurʼan's preservation is the One from whom nothing, spoken aloud or buried in the heart, escapes.

## "And We will make easy for you the easy way" (ayah 8)

The second promise widens from the revelation to the whole mission. Ibn Kathir explains it on two levels at once: 'We will make good deeds and statements easy for you, and We will legislate for you a Law that is easy, tolerant, straight and just — with no crookedness, difficulty or hardship in it.' The "easy way" (*al-yusrā*) is thus the Sharīʿah of Islam itself, described in the Tafsir Summary as "the sacred laws of Islam."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices something subtle in the wording. The context might have led us to expect "We will make the Sharīʿah easy *for you*." Instead the ayah says, literally, "We will facilitate *you* toward the easiest way" — the object of the easing is the Prophet ﷺ himself, not just the path. The reason, Maʿārif suggests, is that Allah would predispose the Prophet ﷺ to the sacred laws so that they became part of his very nature: he would not merely follow the Sharīʿah but become an embodiment of it.

## Reading the passage as one movement

Taken together, the ayat move from the immediate to the lifelong. First: the words themselves are safe (ayah 6). Second: even the apparent exceptions to that safety are governed by the will and complete knowledge of Allah (ayah 7). Third: the one who carries those words will himself be eased — toward a religion with no crookedness, difficulty or hardship in it (ayah 8). Ibn Kathir notes that this sūrah was revealed in Makkah before the migration to Al-Madinah, citing as proof what Al-Bukhari recorded from Al-Baraʼ bin ʿAzib — that he had already learned to recite "Glorify the Name of your Lord, the Most High" from the early Companion-teachers, such as Musʿab bin ʿUmayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, before the Prophet ﷺ himself arrived in Madinah. Only after the promises of ayat 6–8 are given does the command follow in ayah 9: "Therefore remind, in case the reminder profits."

passages.title: Reminding benefits the fearful, the wretched refuse
passages.tafsir:
# The Reminder and the Two Hearts (87:9–13)

After Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that He will make him recite without forgetting and will ease his path (ayat 6–8), He now gives the command those preparations were for: **remind**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection explicit: the preceding verses described the facilities Allah created for the Prophet ﷺ in performing his prophetic obligation, and this verse now commands him to perform it. Then, in four swift verses, the passage sets out the only two responses a reminder can meet — the fearful heart that receives it, and the wretched soul that turns away and walks into the great Fire. One command, two audiences, two destinies.

## "So remind, if the reminder benefits" — is the command conditional?

Ayah 9 reads: *fa-dhakkir in nafaʿati-dh-dhikrā* — "Therefore remind in case the reminder profits." The little word *in* ("if") looks at first like a condition, as though the Prophet ﷺ should only preach when he can predict success. The commentators read it more carefully, from two angles.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** explains that the "if" here is not conditional at all but **emphatic**. Many languages use "if" this way for something that is always true — as when one says, "If you are a man, then you will have to do this work," where his being a man is not in doubt. The verse's real force, on this reading, is: reminding people of truth and righteousness is *certainly* useful — therefore this beneficial thing must never be abandoned at any time.

**Ibn Kathir** draws a complementary lesson from the same wording: "remind where reminding is beneficial." From this, he says, we learn **the etiquette of spreading knowledge — that it should not be wasted upon those who are not suitable or worthy of it**. He cites the Commander of the Believers, ʿAli, who said: "You do not tell people any statement that their intellects do not grasp except that it will be a *fitnah* (trial) for some of them," and also: "Tell people that which they know. Would you like for Allah and His Messenger to be rejected?"

Held together, the two readings give a balanced method: the duty to remind never lapses — but wisdom governs *what* is said, *to whom*, and *when*, so that knowledge illuminates rather than becomes a trial.

## Ayah 10 — the heart that fears will receive it

*Sa-yadhdhakkaru man yakhshā* — "The reminder will be received by him who fears." Ibn Kathir unfolds who this person is: "he whose heart fears Allah and who knows that he is going to meet Him, will receive admonition from what you convey to him, O Muhammad." Notice what makes the reminder land: not intelligence, not eloquence in the preacher, but a prior condition in the listener — awe of Allah joined to the certainty of standing before Him. The reminder does not create that fear from nothing; it finds it, and the fearful heart answers.

## Ayat 11–13 — the wretched who shuns it, and where shunning leads

Against *man yakhshā* stands *al-ashqā* — "the most wretched" — who **avoids** the very reminder that would save him (ayah 11). The passage then follows him to his end: he "will enter the great Fire" (ayah 12), and there — in one of the Qurʼan's most terrifying sentences — "he will neither die nor live" (ayah 13).

Ibn Kathir explains this state: he will not die and thus be allowed to rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him. Instead, his very living will be harmful to him, because it is the means by which he feels the pain of the torment and its various punishments. Existence itself becomes the instrument of the penalty — no relief through death, no life worth the name.

## From the Sunnah — who stays in the Fire, and who comes out

Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded by **Imam Ahmad** from Abu Saʿid, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ distinguished two groups: "Concerning the people of the Fire who are deserving of it, they will not die nor will they live" — these are the ones ayah 13 describes. But regarding people for whom Allah wants mercy, He will cause them to die in the Fire; then the intercessors will be allowed to come to them, and they will be planted in the River of al-Ḥayā (the narrator was unsure of the exact name — al-Ḥayāh, al-Ḥayawān, or the River of Paradise), "and they will sprout up like the sprouting of the seed on the moist bank of a flowing stream." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Haven't you all seen the tree that is green, then it turns yellow, then it turns green again?" — at which some of those present remarked that it was as if the Prophet ﷺ had lived in the desert wilderness, so vivid were his parables of nature.

Ahmad also recorded a second version from Abu Saʿid — **and Muslim recorded it as well** — in which people whom the Fire burns for their sins are caused to die until they become like burnt coal; then intercession is permitted, they are brought out group after group and scattered over the rivers of Paradise, and it is said, "O people of Paradise! Pour down upon them" — and they sprout like a seed on the bank of a flowing stream.

These narrations guard the reader from two errors. Ayah 13's "neither die nor live" belongs to the people of the Fire *who are deserving of it* — the wretched who refused the reminder altogether. It is not the fate of everyone the Fire touches: those for whom Allah wants mercy will be taken out by intercession and restored, tender and new, like green growth after rain. The same passage that closes the door on the wretched quietly leaves it open, by Allah's mercy, for others.

## Living this passage

The passage speaks first to the Prophet ﷺ, but through him to everyone who carries any portion of this religion to others. Two disciplines follow directly from the sources. First, from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: never abandon the reminder on the excuse that it "won't work" — its benefit is affirmed, not conditioned. Second, from Ibn Kathir and ʿAli's counsel: match the word to the listener; do not hand people what their understanding cannot yet carry.

And for the listener, the passage is a mirror with only two faces. Every reminder that reaches you — an ayah recited, an admonition heard — sorts you in that moment into one of the two camps of ayat 10 and 11: the heart that fears Allah and knows it will meet Him, or the wretched soul that turns away. The question the passage presses on every heart is simply: which of the two will you be?

passages.title: True success, worldly preference, and earlier scriptures
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close Sūrah al-Aʿlā with a complete map of salvation in miniature: a two-line description of the person who truly succeeds (ayat 14–15), a diagnosis of the one disease that keeps most people from becoming that person (ayat 16–17), and a striking seal of authority — the declaration that this very teaching was already written in the scriptures given to Ibrāhīm and Mūsā, peace be upon them (ayat 18–19). What holds the passage together is a single contrast: the purified soul that chooses what lasts, against the heedless soul that grabs what is nearest.

## Who succeeds? (ayat 14–15)

Ayah 14 opens with a word of certainty: *qad aflaḥa* — "successful indeed." The success is tied to one thing: *tazakkā*, "he purified himself."

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān opens up the word. *Tazakkā* comes from the same root as *zakāh*, whose primitive meaning is "to purify" — the zakāh of wealth is so named because giving it purifies the rest of a person's wealth for him. Here, Maʿārif explains, the word is used in its widest sense: it embraces purity of faith, purity of character, and purity of wealth all at once. Ibn Kathir puts it in similarly comprehensive terms: the successful person "purifies himself from despised characteristics and follows what Allah has revealed to the Messenger ﷺ." Purification, in other words, is not a vague inner glow; it is cleansing the heart of false belief and low character, and it is measured against revelation.

Ayah 15 then names the outward fruit of that inner state: "and remembers the Name of his Lord, and prays." Ibn Kathir explains this as establishing the prayer in its appointed time, "seeking the pleasure of Allah, obedience to His command, and implementation of His Law." Notice the sequence the ayat themselves draw: first purification, then remembrance of the Lord's Name, then prayer — the cleansed heart remembers, and the remembering heart stands to pray. Maʿārif notes that the prayer here covers every category, obligatory and supererogatory alike; some commentators said it refers especially to the ʿĪd prayers, but that reading still falls comfortably within the general one.

**The early Muslims read charity into these two ayat.** Ibn Kathir records that the Commander of the believers, ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz, used to command the people to give Ṣadaqat al-Fiṭr (the charity due at the end of Ramadan), and he would recite these very two ayat as he did so. Abū al-Aḥwaṣ drew a similar lesson: if a beggar comes to you when you are about to pray, give the charity first, then pray — because Allah put *tazakkā* before *ṣallā*. And Qatādah summarised the pair simply: "He purifies his wealth and pleases his Creator." None of this narrows the ayah to money; it shows how naturally these early Muslims heard both meanings — purity of soul and purity of wealth — inside one word.

## The disease: preferring what is in front of you (ayat 16–17)

Then the address turns, almost abruptly: "But you prefer the life of this world" (ayah 16). The word *bal* ("rather / but") signals the objection: you know all this, and yet you choose otherwise. Ibn Kathir paraphrases: you give this world precedence over the matter of the Hereafter because of what it visibly contains — livelihood, income, profitable gain.

Why do people make so poor a trade? Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān transmits the penetrating answer of the Companion ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd: people prefer the blessings of this world because they are *visible and readily available*, while the blessings of the Hereafter are *invisible and not readily at hand*. People unaware of reality preferred the seen to the unseen — and that preference became the cause of eternal loss. This is why, Maʿārif continues, Allah through His Messengers and Books described the Hereafter so vividly that it is as if one could perceive it through the senses: to rescue people from a mistake of perception, not merely of appetite.

Ayah 17 supplies the correction in four Arabic words: "although the Hereafter is better (*khayr*) and more lasting (*abqā*)." Ibn Kathir presses the logic: this worldly life is lowly and temporal, the Hereafter noble and eternal — so how can an intelligent person prefer the short-lived over the everlasting, and pour his concern into what will soon slip away from him? Maʿārif adds that the ayah is really an appeal to intelligence, and identifies the two incurable defects of every worldly pleasure: even at its peak it is mixed with grief and hardship, and it does not last — "a king of today becomes a pauper tomorrow; a vigorous youth of today becomes old tomorrow." The Hereafter is free of both defects.

Maʿārif drives it home with a homely scenario. Suppose a man is offered two houses: a magnificent, fully furnished mansion — but only for a month or two, after which he must vacate — or a plain, modest house that will be his permanently. Every sensible person takes the second. On that analogy alone, one should prefer the Hereafter even if (for argument's sake) its blessings were inferior — but in fact they are not only permanent, they are also far superior. Only, in Maʿārif's blunt phrase, "an unfortunate fool" would still choose the mansion.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that whoever loves his worldly life harms his Hereafter, and whoever loves his Hereafter harms his worldly life — "therefore choose that which is everlasting over that which is temporal." Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad was alone in recording this hadith. The two loves pull against each other; the Prophet ﷺ does not deny the tension but tells us which side to come down on.

Notice that neither ayah nor commentary demands abandoning the world. The critique is of *īthār* — preference, giving the dunyā first place. The question the passage puts to the reader is not "do you have a share of this world?" but "which of the two do you put first when they compete?"

## An ancient message (ayat 18–19)

The sūrah then closes with a remarkable claim: "Verily, this is in the former Scriptures — the Scriptures of Ibrāhīm and Mūsā."

**What does "this" refer to?** Ibn Kathir reports two views. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said "the story of this sūrah is in the earlier Scriptures" — the whole sūrah's message. Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī preferred a more precise reading: "this" points to the immediately preceding statement, ayat 14–17 — the teaching that success lies in purification, remembrance, and prayer, and that the Hereafter outweighs this world. Ibn Kathir judges aṭ-Ṭabarī's view "good and strong," noting that the like of it is reported from Qatādah and Ibn Zayd — and closes, as the scholars do, with "and Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān holds both possibilities open in the same spirit: either all the themes of the sūrah, or its final theme specifically, stood written in the earlier Scriptures. On which scriptures of Mūsā are meant, Maʿārif again leaves the matter open: possibly scriptures given to him before the Torah, possibly the Torah itself.

The point of the claim is weighty either way. The Qurʼān is telling its first hearers — and us — that this teaching is not a novelty of seventh-century Arabia. The same diagnosis of the human condition and the same prescription were delivered to Ibrāhīm and to Mūsā. Revelation has one moral spine across the ages. Ibn Kathir points out that the Qurʼān makes the identical move in Sūrat an-Najm (53:36–42), where the Scriptures of Mūsā and of "Ibrāhīm who fulfilled" are cited for the principles that no soul bears another's burden, that man has only what he strives for, that his striving will be seen and fully recompensed, and that to your Lord is the final end.

**What was in those scriptures?** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān records a narration transmitted by Ājurrī from Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, who asked the Prophet ﷺ about the contents of the scriptures of Ibrāhīm. He replied that they contained educating parables. One addresses a tyrant king: "You haughty, arrogant and oppressive ruler — I did not give you kingdom so that you may amass wealth; I gave you power so that you may let the supplication of the oppressed reach Me, for My law does not reject the supplication of an oppressed person, even if uttered by an unbeliever." Another parable counsels the ordinary person: a wise man should divide his time into three parts — one for the worship of his Lord and supplication, one for self-assessment of his deeds and reflection on Allah's omnipotence and creation, and one for earning his livelihood and meeting his natural needs. He should stay aware of the circumstances of his time, keep busy with his intended work, and guard his tongue — whoever counts speech among his deeds will speak only when there is real need.

Abū Dharr then asked about the scriptures of Mūsā. The Prophet ﷺ replied that they contained lessons of wisdom, among them a series of astonishments: I am surprised at the one who is certain he will die, yet lives carefree; at the one who believes in divine destiny, yet is despondent and aggrieved; at the one who watches the rise and fall of nations and the turning of fortunes, yet remains content with the world; at the one who believes in the Reckoning of the Hereafter, yet abandons good deeds. Each saying exposes the same gap the sūrah exposes — between what a person professes to believe and how he actually weighs the world.

Finally Abū Dharr asked: has anything from those scriptures been revealed to *you*? The Prophet ﷺ answered yes — and told him to recite these very verses, 14–19 of this sūrah. That narration is the perfect close to the passage: the ayat that declare their own presence in the earlier scriptures are themselves the portion of those scriptures given to this Ummah.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a short, searching checklist drawn straight from its own words: purify — faith, character, and wealth, for *tazakkā* covers all three; remember Allah's Name and guard the prayer in its time; and when this world and the next compete for first place in your heart, remember Ibn Masʿūd's warning that the visible is not the valuable, the mansion-for-a-month analogy, and the Prophet's ﷺ counsel to "choose that which is everlasting over that which is temporal." This is not one sūrah's advice; by Allah's own testimony, it is the message He has been sending since the scriptures of Ibrāhīm and Mūsā.
